messages.subject: legend for geom_errorbar
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I need to plot multiple CIs and compare them ... I manage to do so with a code similar to the example included below. However, I could not find any way to add a Legend to indicate which CI corresponds to which method ... can anyone please advise?

Many thanks in advance,
Best regards,
Giovanni

rm(list=ls())                                              # clear workspace
library(ggplot2)                                           # use ggplot2 library

methodlabels <- c("Classic", "Own Bootstrap",              # prepare plot labels
"R Bootstrap")
errortypelabels <- c("'Normal'", "'Student-t'",            # prepare plot labels
"'Exponential'")
betalabels <- c("'Beta_1'", "'Beta_2'", "'Beta_3'")        # prepare plot labels
betas <- c(1, -2, 3)                                       # my real parameters
set.seed(11)
S <- 100
B <- 50
P <- length(betas)
classiccis <- owncis <- rbootcis <- array(data=0,dim=c(S,1,3,2))
for (p in 1:P) {
classiccis[,1,p,1] <- rnorm(100,mean=betas[p]-1.0,sd=0.5)
classiccis[,1,p,2] <- rnorm(100,mean=betas[p]+1.0,sd=0.5)
owncis[,1,p,1] <- rnorm(100,mean=betas[p]-1.0,sd=0.5)
owncis[,1,p,2] <- rnorm(100,mean=betas[p]+1.0,sd=0.5)
rbootcis[,1,p,1] <- rnorm(100,mean=betas[p]-1.0,sd=0.5)
rbootcis[,1,p,2] <- rnorm(100,mean=betas[p]+1.0,sd=0.5)
}

##
## Function that generates the ggplot of the CI for a given parameter
## and error type
##
ciplot <- function() {
x <- 1:S
y <- rep(betas[p],S)
data <- data.frame(x,y)
classiclimits <- aes(x=x[1:100],ymax = classiccis[1:100,e,p,1],
ymin=classiccis[1:100,e,p,2])
ownlimits <- aes(x=x[1:100]+0.4,ymax = owncis[1:100,e,p,1],
ymin=owncis[1:100,e,p,2])
rbootlimits <- aes(x=x[1:100]+0.8,ymax = rbootcis[1:100,e,p,1],
ymin=rbootcis[1:100,e,p,2])
g1 <- ggplot(data, aes(x=x, y=y))
g1 + geom_errorbar(classiclimits, colour="red") + geom_errorbar(
     ownlimits, colour="green") + geom_errorbar(rbootlimits,
     colour="blue") + geom_hline(yintercept = betas[p]) + xlab(
     "Simulation") + ylab(betalabels[p]) + opts(title = paste("CI for",
     errortypelabels[e],"error, ",betalabels[p],",",S/5,
     "simulations and ",B,"bootstrapped samples"))
}

##
## Execute one by one ... note they have to be global
## otherwise seems that ggplot won't find them.
##
## p - means parameter index
## e - means error type index
##
p=1;e=1;ciplot()
p=2;e=1;ciplot()
p=3;e=1;ciplot()

--

with a variety of variable of interest and I am using facet_grid and
groups to summarise it.

geom_line connects the years either side of the missing years
e.g.

dat<-data.frame(year=c(1981:1988,1993:2010),y=rnorm(26))

p+geom_line(aes(year,y))

When what I really want is missing values for these years e.g.

dat<-data.frame(year=c(1981:2010),y=c(rnorm(8),rep(NA,4),rnorm(18)))
p  <-ggplot(dat)
p+geom_line(aes(year,y))

I would rather not add all the missing values but use the power of
ggplot to deal with them automatically. I see that geom_line can take
x as discrete values sp tried

dat<-
data.frame(year=factor(c(1981:2010),levels=1981:2010),y=c(rnorm(8),rep(NA,
4),rnorm(18)))
p  <-ggplot(dat)
p+geom_line(aes(year,y))+scale_x_discrete()

But this doesn´t seem to do the trick. Is there an easy way to do what

messages.subject: Re: Plotting ESRI shape file in ggplot
messages.subject_clean: Plotting ESRI shape file in ggplot
messages.body_plain:
I use fortify (in the ggplot2 package) to convert shapefiles for
plotting in ggplot.  I'm also new, so I don't know if there's a better
way to go about this.

Example:
shape<-readShapeSpatial("path:/file.shp")
shape2<-fortify(shape, region="key")
shape2<-shape2[order(shape2$order), ]
ggplot(data=shape2, aes(long, lat, group=group)) + geom_polygon()
+coord_map()

It seems you can now use xlim & ylim in coord_map to zoom in! Also,
sometimes geom_path seems to work better than geom_polygon.

The "key" is the grouping variable for each contiguous region. I have
run into trouble when a single key in the shapefile refers to multiple
areas (e.g. islands that are all coded as a single region in the
shapefile)--then I try to create a unique value for each region by
combining variables in the shapefile.

It produces really attractive maps, though. Definitely worth the extra
steps over plotting a shapefile directly.

Matt

I seem to have hit upon a case where the scales="free" argument to
facet_grid does absolutely nothing. See the reproducible example below

here, since my y-axis is a factor? I would have thought it became
cartesian "under the hood", or something, i.e., those y-axis ticks are
underlyingly integers (how else get a 2D grid?).

Anyway, I'm writing for two reasons. First, to vote for fixing this
bug :). Second, to ask for advice in working around it. I imagine I
could kluge something together with subplots, but is it possible to do
something nicer, like manually adjusting each facet's x-axis through
the low-level grid API? I don't know anything about grid, so if it is
possible, a concrete example would be useful.

Anyway, thanks for any advice. I love ggplot2, btw!
- Max

See the example below. It would be convenient if the sd value could be
label in each pair of figures.

library(cluster)
png('main.png',width=1000,height=1000)
par(mfrow=c(3,4))
lapply(
  seq(0,1,0.2)
  , function(sd) {
    x=rbind(
      cbind(
        rnorm(10,0,sd)
        , rnorm(10,0,sd)
        , rnorm(10,0,sd)
        )
      , cbind(
        rnorm(15,5,sd)
        , rnorm(15,5,sd)
        , rnorm(15,5,sd)
        )
      )
    plot(pam(x, 2))
  }
  )
dev.off()

messages.body_plain:
Aha, yes, that does it, though I suppose it would be more tricky if I
had more than one column (and wanted the columns to correspond to some
variable).

I didn't realize that scales="free" for facet_grid would only give one
horizontal axis per column (and one vertical axis per row), rather
than free axes in each panel. If that's the intended behavior, that's
cool, but it should be better documented. help(facet_grid) only says
"You can also choose whether the scales should be constant across all
panels (the default), or whether they should be allowed to vary." That
wording suggests to me that scales="free" would allow scales to vary
across *all panels*, not just across columns/rows.

Anyway, thanks for the quick and helpful response!

-Max

messages.subject: Funny variable names in ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
This works fine:

ggplot(data.frame(a=1:10,b=1:10)) + geom_line(aes(x=a,y=b))

This gives an error:

> ggplot(data.frame(`a b`=1:10,b=1:10)) + geom_line(aes(x=`a b`,y=b))
Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'a ' not found

As far as I can tell, `a b` is a perfectly correct R identifier (name):

> class(quote(`a b`))
[1] "name"
> `a b` <- 234
> `a b`
[1] 234

messages.subject: Re: Plotting ESRI shape file in ggplot
messages.subject_clean: Plotting ESRI shape file in ggplot
messages.body_plain:
How, if at all, does fortify handle holes in polygons?

I came across this a while back as I wrote my own conversion functions
with a similar purpose. Either fortify didn't exist back then or I
just didn't find it. Anyway, once I got a hold of the difficult data
structures returned by readShape*, it was fairly easy to convert
shapefiles with points and lines. Also polygons that you intend to
plot as a border with geom_path were easy enough to convert, but if
you want to fill polygons, then holes cannot be separate, but rather
they need to be attached to the outer border. And those attaching
segments need to be added.

Another thing I noticed was that shapefiles are often too large to be
manipulated in memory. The readShape* functions read the whole shape
database into memory, which is often enough to use all available
memory. Nothing I could do about that, but I found it better to
implement conversion functions as shapefile to CSV-file conversions
writing one shape at a time to a file instead of manipulating large
data frames in memory.

If you use scale_shape_manual, you need to select shapes that have a
fill value (that was done automatically by scale_shape(solid=TRUE).
For instance,

ggplot(all_data, aes(x=x_val, y=y_val,   color=case, shape=case, fill=case))+
 geom_point(size=4)+
 geom_point(size=2, fill="white")+
 geom_line()+
 scale_shape_manual("Network", breaks=lbls, labels=lbls, values=c(21, 24)) +
scale_colour_manual("Network", breaks=lbls, labels=lbls, values=c(1,2)) +
scale_fill_manual("Network", breaks=lbls, labels=lbls, values=c(1,2))

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Plotting ESRI shape file in ggplot
messages.subject_clean: Plotting ESRI shape file in ggplot
messages.body_plain:
> How, if at all, does fortify handle holes in polygons?

It returns them as independent polygons with hole = TRUE.  Then it's
up to you to draw them on top of the land with the appropriate
colours.  I know that this isn't the best way to deal with them, but
it's simple and it works for most maps I've come across.

> Another thing I noticed was that shapefiles are often too large to be
> manipulated in memory. The readShape* functions read the whole shape
> database into memory, which is often enough to use all available
> memory. Nothing I could do about that, but I found it better to
> implement conversion functions as shapefile to CSV-file conversions
> writing one shape at a time to a file instead of manipulating large
> data frames in memory.

That's a good point, but if the shapefiles are too big to fit in
memory, then I think you're going to have problems drawing them
because of the very high resolution.

Hadley

messages.subject_clean: Error in if (!all(data$ymin == 0)) warning("Stacking not well defined when ymin != 0", : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
messages.body_plain:
I was using the following code successfully until I added a vast
quantity of data.  At which point I started getting the error:

Error in if (!all(data$ymin == 0)) warning("Stacking not well defined when ymin != 0",  :
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

My function (graph8by2) just uses the summary function to create some
factors and the creates a faceted bar chart.  I'm fairly new and don't
really understand what the error is telling me and I can't really send
a sample of the data since it worked when it was small and doesn't now
that it's big.  Anyway I just thought if anyone had a guess as to
where I should begin looking for problems in the morning (I live in
Spain) then that'd be helpful.  Thanks in advance to any responders.

I probably should mention that I did get the warning about "Stacking
not well defined" earlier, but since I wasn't stacking the bars and
the graphs appeared to be coming out fine I ignored it.  The "missing
value where TRUE/FALSE needed" is new but the variables have always
had some missing values so it is not really clear what that means or
what is different.

graph8by2 <- function( var1, var2, dep, data) {

 temp1 <- summary(data[,var1])
 temp2 <- summary(data[,var2])
 fac1 <- factor(cut(data[,var1] ,
    breaks=c(temp1["Min."], temp1["1st Qu."]-((temp1["Median"]-temp1["1st Qu."])/2),
             temp1["1st Qu."], temp1["Median"]-((temp1["Median"]-temp1["1st Qu."])/2),
             temp1["Median"], temp1["Median"]+((temp1["3rd Qu."]-temp1["Median"])/2),
             temp1["3rd Qu."], temp1["3rd Qu."]+((temp1["3rd Qu."]-temp1["Median"])/2),
             temp1["Max."]) ))
 fac2 <- factor(cut(data[,var2] ,
    breaks=c(temp2["Min."], temp2["1st Qu."]-((temp2["Median"]-temp2["1st Qu."])/2),
             temp2["1st Qu."], temp2["Median"]-((temp2["Median"]-temp2["1st Qu."])/2),
             temp2["Median"], temp2["Median"]+((temp2["3rd Qu."]-temp2["Median"])/2),
             temp2["3rd Qu."], temp2["3rd Qu."]+((temp2["3rd Qu."]-temp2["Median"])/2),
             temp2["Max."]) ))

 temp3 <- aggregate(data[, dep] ,
    list( var1 =fac1, var2 =fac2),
    mean)
 temp4 <- aggregate(data[, dep] ,
    list( var1 =fac1, var2 =fac2 ),
    length)
 temp4 <- as.vector(temp4$x)

 temp3$sample.size <- factor(cut(temp4 ,  breaks=c(0, 100, 1000, 5000, 1000000 ) ))

 qplot(var1, x, fill= sample.size, geom="bar", facets= var2 ~ . ,  data= temp3,
    xlab = var1 , ylab = paste(dep," faceted by ", var2) ,
    main = paste(dep, "\n by", var1, ",", var2) )
}

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gerry,

Ok, there are two problems with your code:

 * There's a bug so that when you set data = NULL, the layer still
uses the default dataset
 * When you set mapping = NULL that means (by design), just use the
defaults - you want (outside of aes) inherit.aes = FALSE

The easiest way to resolve both of these problems is to create another
data frame that specifies the different ranges and their colours. Then
use geom_rect with that dataset.  Also note that you can use -Inf and
Inf to refer to the left and right extents of the plotting area
respectively.

Hadley

messages.subject: geom_jitter()
messages.body_plain:
Dear ggplot2 group

I am working at a pharmaceutical company and am moving the data visualisation component from a variety of methods to the ggplot2 framework.

I am a little surprised to find something a little strange with geom_jitter(). In my department a boxplot with jittered data points is rather critical plot for many analyses so that the distributions of data points underlying the plot can be questioned.

Let us consider the following code

library(ggplot2)
data <- cbind(as.data.frame(cbind(NULL, rep(LETTERS[1:8],8))),rnorm(64))
colnames(data) <- c("class", "signal")
print(ggplot(data, aes(class, signal)) + geom_boxplot() + geom_jitter())

I create a data.frame with 8 "experimental classes", each of which has 8 measurements.
This is plotted as a boxplot with jitter. Everything looks pretty OK. However when I run the code one of the classes often has more jittered dots than it has observations within the data. In most graphs there is at least one class with 9 dots, in some cases a column with 10 data points is seen.

Does anyone else see this problem? Is there something fundamentally stupid that I am doing. I have checked several times and it is not just the case that I can't count! This is seen using both OSX ggplot2_0.8.5 and 64bit linux with ggplot2_0.8.7.

Thanks, greetings from Finland

Stephen

messages.subject: RE: geom_jitter()
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stephen,

Notice that you plot your data twice: once as a boxplots and once as a
jitter plot. Suppose you have 9 observations of which one is an outlier.
The boxplot will display that outliers as a point. The jitter geom plots
a point for each observation. Hence you end up with 10 points (9 from
jitter, 1 from boxplot). Try putting the jitter points in a different
color or shape. Then you'll see the difference.

HTH,

Thierry

PS Boxplots might not be a very good idea if you have only 9
observations...

messages.subject_clean: Plotting ESRI shape file in ggplot
messages.body_plain:
On 5.5.2010 23:37, hadley wickham wrote:
> It returns them as independent polygons with hole = TRUE.  Then it's
> up to you to draw them on top of the land with the appropriate
> colours.  I know that this isn't the best way to deal with them, but
> it's simple and it works for most maps I've come across.

For most cases it does work, yes, but sometimes you need to be able to
see the background through the holes.

The PBSmapping package [1] provides a findPolys function which can be
used to find the outer polygon to match a hole, or actually a point,
which can be any node of the hole polygon. findPolys deals with similar
data frames as ones that are usable with ggplot.

  [1] http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/PBSmapping/index.html

--
Osmo Salomaa <osmo.s...@strafica.fi>
Strafica Oy <http://www.strafica.fi/>

messages.subject: Annotate facet_grid in panel coordinates instead of data coordinates?
messages.subject_clean: Annotate facet_grid in panel coordinates instead of data coordinates?
messages.body_plain:
I am using facet_grid to create a 2D grid of scatter plots. Each plot
has a linear regression line. I'm annotating each panel with the
correlation coefficient. I'm using scales="free". I'd like to place
the annotations in a consistent location within each panel, e.g. the
upper left corner. In other words, I'd like to place the annotations
using the coordinates of the panel as opposed to the coordinates of
the data in the panel. Is there any way to do this?

For an example of the "problem," with the annotations placed in data
coordinates, please see:
http://gist.github.com/392102

Thanks,
AdamK

--

messages.subject: Set ticks independently for each axis?
messages.subject_clean: Set ticks independently for each axis?
messages.body_plain:
I guess this is a feature request:

It would be nice to be able to set the ticks independently for each
axis. Since the axis.text and axis.title are independent for each
axis, why not the ticks as well? And while we're at it, how about the
axis.line also? In general, why not make each axis seperately
customizable?

I realize there may be a "consistency" argument to generally want to
avoid this, but there are cases, particularly when using grid.layout
to place multiple graphs on a page, where indepedent control of the
axes would be mighty handy.

Thanks,
AdamK

Is there a way to query the plot itself about what the range will be for each facet, so that the code doesn't have to know what particular data will be displayed?

Thanks,
AdamK

messages.subject: Re: Missing values in geom_line
messages.body_plain:
> Many thanks, my problem was partly laziness. The example I gave was a
> sinplified one as my data.frame  had many covariates coming from a glm that
> wasn´t a balanced design.

This should be easy to fix with application of expand.grid and merge.

I guess the only way is to preprocess the data.
> But am I right in thinking that you can´t use factors as the x variable in
> geom_line?
> As I had thought that
>
> dat<-data.frame(x=factor(c(1991:2000,2005:2010),levels=1991:2010),y=rnorm(16))
> ggplot(dat)+geom_line(aes(x,y))
>
> would work as x can be discrete and factor does imply an order.

By default, ggplot2 uses all the factors displayed on the plot to
generate groups - i.e. you get one line for every combination of
categorical values.  This obviously doesn't work here, so you need to
manually override it:

ggplot(dat)+geom_line(aes(x,y, group = 1))

Hadley

messages.subject_clean: Set ticks independently for each axis?
messages.body_plain:
In adition to setting ticks independently for each axis, it would be
nice to be able to be able to specify irregularly-spaced points for
tick marks. Yesterday wanted to plot observations at 3, 6, 12, 18, 24,
36, 48, 60, and 72 months. I was happy with the standard gridlines,
but I wanted to have ticks & labels at the points where I had data
(especially since some timepoints are missing from some graphs). So
far as I can tell, in all of R (or S) the only way to do this would be
to print the labels and tick marks as calls to very low level
functions (place text here, know exactly where "here" is, etc.). It
would be sweet if xaxp or something allowed the user to specify a
vector of tick locations for cases like this.

Patrick

messages.subject: Re: sub-setting in order to facet_grid properly
messages.subject_clean: sub-setting in order to facet_grid properly
messages.body_plain:
If you want to facet by the pollen treatment and fruit/seed then each
row in your dataframe needs to correspond to one avg and se for a
single pollen treatment and either fruit or seed (as opposed to a
different columns for fruit and seed) and a variable identifying if
this is a fruit or seed measurement on which to facet.

Try this:
pollin.m <- melt(pollin2, measure.vars = c("fruit","seed"))

pollin.m.avg <- ddply(pollin.m,
  c("treat","pollen", "emasc","bag","pobag","variable"),
  function(df) {
    c(avg=mean(df$value, na.rm = TRUE), se=std.error(df$value))
  })

ggplot(pollin.m.avg, aes(emasc, avg, ymin = avg - se, ymax=avg + se) )+
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_errorbar(width=0.15)+
  facet_grid(variable ~ pobag, scale = "free_y")

Charlotte

messages.subject: Question about coord_trans (possibly bug 75)
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I have a problem with the coord_trans function. Here's a reproducible
plot the looks fine:

dsmall = diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds),1000),]
c <- ggplot(dsmall, aes(clarity, price, colour = factor(color)))
c  + stat_summary(fun.ymin=min,fun.ymax=max, geom="errorbar")

Now if I want to transform the y axis to log scale, the x axis gets
messed up:

dsmall = diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds),1000),]
c <- ggplot(dsmall, aes(clarity, price, colour = factor(color)))
c  + stat_summary(fun.ymin=min,fun.ymax=max, geom="errorbar")
+coord_trans(y="log")

After some searching, I found that is could possibly be bug 75.
(http://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/issue/75)

Is that correct? And if yes, @hadley any idea when this might be
fixed? Of course everybody wants their bugs fixed first, but it seems
to me that a log transformation of the y axis is one of the most
common transformation in scientific plots. I'm also curious to learn
if theres a way around it with the current version (ggplot2_0.8.7).

Thanks!
Marcel

--

messages.subject: Scaling & Stats Bug
messages.body_plain:
Hey all

I continue to run into problems with logs. Let's say I have a simple
data frame, like

df = data.frame(x=c(1,1,1),y=c(1,0,0.5))

The mean of df$y is 0.5:

> mean(df$y)
[1] 0.5

Plotting this with a log10 transformed y axis shows an incorrect value
(somewhere around 10^-0.33):

> ggplot(df,aes(x,y)) + stat_summary(fun.y=mean, geom="point") + scale_y_continuous(trans="log10")

but it should be 10^-0.30103 since

> log10(mean(df$y))
[1] -0.30103

Now even stranger, when I add 0.01 to the y values:

> df$y = df$y+0.01
> mean(df$y)
[1] 0.51

I would now expect the mean value to be at 10^-0.2924298 since

> log10(mean(df$y))
[1] -0.2924298

but

> ggplot(df,aes(x,y)) + stat_summary(fun.y=mean, geom="point") + scale_y_continuous(trans="log10")

shows it completely off, around 10^-0.75

Repeat the entire exercise without  scale_y_continuous(trans="log10"),
and everything works perfectly fine.

After reading up on scales and statistical transformations, it seems
clear to me that scale transforms the data BEFORE the statistical
summary. So what is does is take the mean of log10(0.01), log10(0.51)
and log10(1.01) which is -0.7627027. Fair enough, but why is the mean
now shown as 10^-0.7627027 (rather than just -0.7627027)? If this
behavior is intended, I'd love to hear the reasoning behind it.
Otherwise it's probably a bug.

Thanks!
Marcel

--

messages.body_plain:
Regarding the second example.  The scale has been transformed but the
plotted raw data haven't.  So, the original point y = 0.01 is plotted
at 10^{-2}, and explains why the mean is at 10^(-0.76) - it's the
backtransformed mean of log10(y).

The problem with the first example is that infinity gets involved.
> log10(df$y)
[1]  0.00000     -Inf -0.30103
> mean(log10(df$y))
[1] -Inf

So, in the plot coordinate system the mean gets the y-coordinate -Inf
which refers to the bottom most margin of the plot about 10^-0.33
(often a useful trick but here it is misleading).  An illustration of
this behaviour:

ggplot(df,aes(x, y)) + stat_summary(fun.y=mean, geom="point", size = 3) +
 scale_y_continuous(trans="log10") + geom_point(colour = "red")

ggplot(df,aes(x, y)) + stat_summary(fun.y=mean, geom="point", size = 3) +
 scale_y_continuous(trans="log10", limits = c(0.000001, 1)) +
geom_point(colour = "red")

I think I've explained the behavior you've seen but not the philosophy
behind it.  Perhaps Hadley will way in.

Charlotte

messages.subject_clean: xlim(), stat_bin, the group aesthetic and discrete scales
messages.body_plain:
(Trying a more specific list, apologies to r-help@ subscribers that may have already seen this.)

I'm a new ggplot user and am really loving it so far, but I have run into a little trouble.  I'm hoping someone here can clarify.

I've been plotting histograms of discrete variables like so:

> df<-data.frame(names=c("Bob","Mary","Joe","Bob","Bob"))
> p<-ggplot(df,aes(names))
> p+geom_histogram()

But sometimes I want to constrain the categories (the factor in my real dataset has many, many levels).  When I do this in (what seems like) the simplest way I get an error:

> p+geom_histogram()+xlim("Bob","Mary")
Error in data.frame(count = as.numeric(tapply(weight, bins, sum, na.rm = TRUE))$
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 0, 1

If I use xlim() to specify all the levels, or all the levels plus a few extra levels, things work as expected:

> p+geom_histogram()+xlim("Bob","Mary","Joe")
> p+geom_histogram()+xlim("Bob","Mary","Joe","Frank")

I found the error surprising because I had been successfully plotting ..density.. instead of the default ..count.. and constraining the x-axis like so:

> p+geom_histogram(aes(y=..density..,group=1))+xlim("Bob","Mary")

After some experimentation, I've come to the conclusion that using the group aesthetic is the key to successfully using xlim() with stat_bin and discrete scales.  That is, the following does what I want:

p+geom_histogram(aes(group=1))+xlim("Bob","Mary")

I have two questions:

1) Is this expected behavior?  The interaction of the group aesthetic and discrete scale manipulation seems unintuitive to me, but perhaps this is because I'm a ggplot novice.

2) More generally, how do people debug gpplot commands?  When I get a cryptic error message like the above it's nearly always because I've asked for something unreasonable, but if often takes me a long time and lots of experimentation to spot my error. Do folks have any ggplot debugging tips?

Thanks very much for your help,

-J

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, May 11, 2010 at 10:51 AM, John Rauser <jra...@gmail.com> wrote:

> (Trying a more specific list, apologies to r-help@ subscribers that may have already seen this.)
>
> I'm a new ggplot user and am really loving it so far, but I have run into a little trouble.  I'm hoping someone here can clarify.
>
> I've been plotting histograms of discrete variables like so:
>
> > df<-data.frame(names=c("Bob","Mary","Joe","Bob","Bob"))
> > p<-ggplot(df,aes(names))
> > p+geom_histogram()

Firstly, a histogram is intended for numeric data; you want a bar chart instead.
Secondly, xlim() [and ylim()] are *numeric* scales, not categorical. How do you scale 'Bob' and 'Mary'?
To put it another way, what's the numerical 'distance' between Bob and Mary that is necessary
for a histogram routine to rationally proceed? The fact that it 'worked' at all is because R assigns
numerical (integer) codes to different levels of factors (look at str(df)), where the codes are
assigned in lexicographic order.

To restrict the 'scale' in your bar chart, subset your data accordingly before constructing the plot
and then redefine the factor variable (names) to drop unused factor levels before plotting.

I respectfully suggest that you educate yourself about the concept of measurement scales, starting
with the distinctions among nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio scales of data. There is a copious amount
of material on the web to assist you in this enterprise.

As far as subselecting categories in R, look into the %in% function  [type ?%in% at the R prompt]

HTH,
Dennis

>
> But sometimes I want to constrain the categories (the factor in my real dataset has many, many levels).  When I do this in (what seems like) the simplest way I get an error:
>
> > p+geom_histogram()+xlim("Bob","Mary")
> Error in data.frame(count = as.numeric(tapply(weight, bins, sum, na.rm = TRUE))$
>   arguments imply differing number of rows: 0, 1
>
> If I use xlim() to specify all the levels, or all the levels plus a few extra levels, things work as expected:
>
> > p+geom_histogram()+xlim("Bob","Mary","Joe")
> > p+geom_histogram()+xlim("Bob","Mary","Joe","Frank")
>
> I found the error surprising because I had been successfully plotting ..density.. instead of the default ..count.. and constraining the x-axis like so:
>
> > p+geom_histogram(aes(y=..density..,group=1))+xlim("Bob","Mary")
>
> After some experimentation, I've come to the conclusion that using the group aesthetic is the key to successfully using xlim() with stat_bin and discrete scales.  That is, the following does what I want:
>
> p+geom_histogram(aes(group=1))+xlim("Bob","Mary")
>
> I have two questions:
>
> 1) Is this expected behavior?  The interaction of the group aesthetic and discrete scale manipulation seems unintuitive to me, but perhaps this is because I'm a ggplot novice.
>
> 2) More generally, how do people debug gpplot commands?  When I get a cryptic error message like the above it's nearly always because I've asked for something unreasonable, but if often takes me a long time and lots of experimentation to spot my error. Do folks have any ggplot debugging tips?
>
> Thanks very much for your help,
>
> -J
>

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, May 11, 2010 at 1:35 PM, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Firstly, a histogram is intended for numeric data; you want a bar chart instead.

Terminology aside, geom_histogram() is merely a synonym for geom_bar(stat="bin").  See the opening sentence of: http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_histogram.html.  Also:

> p+geom_bar(stat="bin")

> Secondly, xlim() [and ylim()] are *numeric* scales, not categorical. How do you scale 'Bob' and 'Mary'?

I don't think you are correct.  My understanding is that xlim() is simply a helper function that sets the limit parameter of whatever scale you've got.  stat_bin seems to be perfectly happy to work on categorical data, the online docs even provide nice examples (http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/stat_bin.html), as does Dr. Wickham's lovely book.  Further, the online docs also give nice examples of using limits= and xlim() with scale_discrete (http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/scale_discrete.html).  So, near as I can tell, these are equivalent:

> p+geom_bar(stat="bin")+scale_x_discrete(limits=c("Bob","Joe","Mary"))
> p+geom_bar(stat="bin")+xlim("Bob","Joe","Mary")

Indeed this gives me my (now worked around) error:

> p+geom_bar(stat="bin")+scale_x_discrete(limits=c("Bob","Joe"))

Error in data.frame(count = as.numeric(tapply(weight, bins, sum, na.rm = TRUE))$
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 0, 1

>
> I respectfully suggest that you educate yourself...

Right... thanks for that.

I remain confused about the interaction between the group aesthetic and discrete scales (or some deeper thing that I can't yet fathom).  I have worked around my problem, so I'm mostly looking the understand more completely.  I'd be very appreciative if someone could help with that.

Best,

-J

--

messages.body_plain:
Good day all,

Discovered ggplot2 last week and I'm since a big fan, albeit one
that's only on Chapter 5 of the book.. This is my first post, so
apologies for any errors. I'll base it on a 'template' I've seen after
searching the mailing list.

==Goal:
I'm trying to plot a horizontal bar chart, whose bar widths differ in
size.

==Minimal Sample Data/Code:
myData<-data.frame(Group=LETTERS[1:9],
	Size=seq(100,4000,length.out=9),Growth=seq(30,-20,length.out=9))
myP<-ggplot(myData,aes(Group,Growth,size=Size))
# Draw a horizontal bar chart
myP+geom_bar()+coord_flip()

==Output
The bars' widths are all the same. I realise this may not be the
appropriate geom to use and tried:

myP+geom_line()

but that didn't show anything on the layer and instead shows a legend
with Sizes..

Any help on this would be much appreciated.

Regards,

Jorge.

ganges_subbasin_a2pre), and the structure of that data.frame (assuming
it is a data.frame since you are using d*ply on it) has a lot to do
with your problem.  However, I have a few guesses.

I assume ganges_subbasin_a2pre$Month is a character variable.  ddply
turns it into a factor, and factors by default alphabetically order
their levels, and ggplot2 uses the level order by default for
factors.  One way to get around this is to turn ganges_subbasin_a2pre
$Month into a factor yourself with the levels in proper chronological
order.  Then this order would be preserved.  Alternatively, you can
convert your month information into a continuous date-like variable
(zoo::yearmon seems like it might be appropriate for you) and then it
will be treated as a continuous time scale.

--Brian Diggs

messages.subject: Dendrograms / tree models
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

As a newbie on this mailing list, let me first congratulate Hadley and
the ggplot community with creating a truly wonderful piece of graphic
software.

As part of my work I need to create compelling graphic displays of
dendrograms, such as the output produced by tree() and hclust().  Much
to my surprise, a google search for ggplot dendrogram reveals nothing
useful.

So I decided to write some code to plot regression/classification
trees, i.e. the output of tree() in library(tree).

I would be interested to know whether there are better ways of doing
this.  In particular, I created a fortify method for objects of class
tree.  This creates the data frame for plotting the lines.  But I also
need two additional data frames, one for the text labels, and one for
the value labels.  Is there a sensible way of merging the data frames
in such a way that a subset gets used by geom_segment, and another
subset by geom_text?

Andrie

# Plots tree object in ggplot2

fortify.tree <- function(model, data, ...){
  require(tree)
  # Uses tree:::treeco to extract data frame of plot locations
    xy <- tree:::treeco(model)
    n <- model$frame$n

  # Lines copied from tree:::treepl
    x <- xy$x
    y <- xy$y
    node = as.numeric(row.names(model$frame))
    parent <- match((node%/%2), node)
    sibling <- match(ifelse(node%%2, node - 1L, node + 1L), node)

    linev <- data.frame(x=x, y=y, xend=x, yend=y[parent], n=n)
    lineh <- data.frame(x=x[parent], y=y[parent], xend=x,
yend=y[parent], n=n)

    rbind(linev[-1,], lineh[-1,])
}

label.tree <- function(model, ...){
  require(tree)
  # Uses tree:::treeco to extract data frame of plot locations
  xy <- tree:::treeco(model)
  label <- model$frame$var
  sleft  <- model$frame$splits.cutleft
  sright <- model$frame$splits.right

  # Lines copied from tree:::treepl
  x <- xy$x
  y <- xy$y
  node = as.numeric(row.names(model$frame))
  parent <- match((node%/%2), node)
  sibling <- match(ifelse(node%%2, node - 1L, node + 1L), node)

  data <- data.frame(x=x, y=y, label=label)
  data <- data[data$label != "<leaf>",]
  data
}

label.tree.leaf <- function(model, ...){
  require(tree)
  # Uses tree:::treeco to extract data frame of plot locations
  xy <- tree:::treeco(model)
  label <- model$frame$var
  yval  <- model$frame$yval
  sleft  <- model$frame$splits.cutleft
  sright <- model$frame$splits.right

  # Lines copied from tree:::treepl
  x <- xy$x
  y <- xy$y
  node = as.numeric(row.names(model$frame))
  parent <- match((node%/%2), node)
  sibling <- match(ifelse(node%%2, node - 1L, node + 1L), node)

  data <- data.frame(x, y, label, yval)
  data <- data[data$label == "<leaf>",]
  data$label <- round(data$yval, 2)
  data
}

################
# Example code #
################

library(ggplot2)
library(tree)

data(cpus, package="MASS")
cpus.ltr <- tree(log10(perf) ~ syct+mmin+mmax+cach+chmin+chmax, cpus)

p <- ggplot(data=cpus.ltr)
p <- p +
geom_segment(aes(x=x,y=y,xend=xend,yend=yend,size=n),colour="blue",
alpha=0.5)
p <- p + scale_size("n", to=c(0, 3))
p <- p + geom_text(data=label.tree(cpus.ltr), aes(x=x, y=y,
label=label), vjust=-0.5, size=4)
p <- p + geom_text(data=label.tree.leaf(cpus.ltr), aes(x=x, y=y,
label=label), vjust=0.5, size=3)
theme_null <- theme_update(panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),
                           panel.grid.minor = theme_blank(),
                           axis.text.x = theme_blank(),
                           axis.text.y = theme_blank(),
                           axis.ticks = theme_blank(),
                           axis.title.x = theme_blank(),
                           axis.title.y = theme_blank(),
                           legend.position = "none")

p <- p + theme_set(theme_null)
print(p)

messages.subject: Re: Bar chart with differing bar widths.
messages.subject_clean: Bar chart with differing bar widths.
messages.body_plain:
The solution turns out to be elementary (I guess that's why no one
bothered to reply...). Basically, one needs to plot one bar at a time
and specify its width. It's done manually below but a loop with a
properly scaled bar width variable would do.

Sample code:

myData<-data.frame(Group=LETTERS[1:9],
	Size=seq(100,4000,length.out=9),Growth=seq(30,-20,length.out=9))

myP<-ggplot(myData,aes(Group,Growth))
myP+geom_bar(aes(Group,Growth),data=myData[1,],width=0.01*myData[1,"Size"])
last_plot()+geom_bar(aes(Group,Growth),data=myData[2,],width=0.01*myData[2,"Size"])
etc.

Hope this helps whoever needs to do this one day.

messages.subject: Re: Bar chart with differing bar widths.
messages.subject_clean: Bar chart with differing bar widths.
messages.body_plain:
I looked at it earlier and couldn't get anything to work.  That's why
I didn't reply.  I was waiting for someone more knowledgeable.

Your solution is not very elegant; but don't take that as being
harsh.  You at least got something that worked which is better than
what I got.

I played with it some more and finally got an error message that made
sense and got me on the track to something that worked.

ggplot(myData, aes(Group, Growth, width=0.001*Size)) +
geom_bar(stat="identity", position="identity") +
coord_flip()

I bumped the width down two orders of magnitude so it would be more
reasonable.  Width can be an aesthetic, controlled by the data, so it
can be in the original aes().  What you were missing is that with pre-
summarized data, you need a stat="identity" argument to geom_bar.
Otherwise, it tries to summarize (bin) the data for you.  Also,
apparently, "position_stack requires constant width", so I added a
position="identity" argument as well.  Since there is only one set of
data, there is no difference in the positions.

Hadley, why is width not documented in geom_bar? (help page or
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_bar.html )  Is it experimental and
interactions like this have not been worked out, or is that an
oversight?

--Brian Diggs

Hi Brian,

thank you for taking the time to respond. Clearly my presumption
earlier that elementary questions are not answered was wrong and will,
in the future, be more patient and won't be afraid to post no matter
how trivial.

- You have highlighted something important below re the 'width'
argument -- I basically discovered it by luck when looking at some
other person's post.

scaled 'width' variable (say 0.1 to 1) that maps the data one wishes
to plot with the width of the bars. I found that linear interpolation
between the data points i.e minimum value = 0.1, max value = 1,
produces better results than a random scaling factor.

Thanks once again,

Jorge.

messages.subject_clean: Technique for multiple x axis merely for user viewing
messages.body_plain:
Chris

Quoting from the ggplot2 book, page 166:  "There is no way to produce
a plot with two axes in ggplot2 because this type of plot is
fundamentally misleading".

What you want to do is slightly different though, so here is one
workaround.  The idea is to modify the scale labels to display
temperaturs in Celsius as well as Fahrenheit:

degC <- seq(0,100,10)
degCandF <- paste(degC,"C / ",degC * 9 / 5 + 32,"F",sep="")

d <- data.frame(tempcelcius=round(rnorm(25,15, 10),
1),attendence=rnorm(25,500, 100))

p <- qplot(x=tempcelcius,y=attendence,data=d)
p <- p + scale_x_continuous("Temperature (Celsius/
Fahrenheit)",breaks=degC,labels=degCandF)
print(p)

--

Andrie

messages.subject: Help with polygons
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

My goal is to create a Voronoi Tessellation which is bounded by the
borders of the United States and Canada, then export the polygons to a
dataframe for plotting in ggplot2. After much futzing around with
spatstat and sp, I've given up on figuring out how to do this the
right way. I got this far:

cities <- structure(list(CitState = c("SiouxFalls SD", "Rockford IL",
"Kenosha WI",
"Duluth MN", "SiouxCity IA", "CedarRapids IA", "NewYork NY"),
    Latitude = c(43.54599, 42.265973, 42.577791, 46.779135,
42.489678,
    41.976662, 40.756054), Longitude = c(-96.731291, -89.086667,
    -87.822644, -92.108243, -96.404948, -91.673155, -73.986951
    )), .Names = c("CitState", "Latitude", "Longitude"), row.names =
c(1L,
2L, 3L, 4L, 5L, 6L, 267L), class = "data.frame")

library(maps)
library(spatstat)
us <- data.frame(map("usa", regions = "main",plot = F)[c("x","y")])
manhattan <- data.frame(map("usa", regions = "manhattan",plot = F)
[c("x","y")])
spatstat.options(checkpolygons = FALSE)
us.win <- owin(poly = list(list(x = us$x, y = us$y),list(x = manhattan
$x,y = manhattan$y)))
us.ppp <- ppp(cities$Longitude, cities$Latitude, window = us.win)
us.d <- dirichlet(us.ppp)

Extracting polygons from the output of dirichlet() seems hopeless.

So, I'm wondering if I can fake it. I can create a voronoi
tessellation from my data with deldir(), and get that into the right
shape for plotting. I'm wondering if there is some way to plot the
inverse of the us as a polygon, plotted over the voronoi tessellation,
making it appear to be bounded by the borders of the us.

us$ID <- 1
ggplot(us, aes(x,y)) + geom_polygon(aes(group = ID))

-Joe

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I managed to get a background color shading for your plot, but the
variable legend got messed up in the process. Hopefully someone
can rescue that for you.

I did some rearrangement of your plot calls, and created a small data frame to
contain some information for years (I'm assuming 2008-2009, but I could be
wrong...). The following is loosely modeled on the unemployment data graph in
section 5.10, p. 86 of the ggplot2 book.

# Small data frame to contain a factor for which background colors are
# to be mapped, plus a start and end vector of x-values (WEEK). The value
# 5.5 is to provide an illusion of continuity in color - otherwise, there will be a gap
ydata <- data.frame(year = factor(c(2008, 2009)), start = c(1, 5.5),
                    end = c(5.5, 53))

# Removed fill = variable and took out the x-scale
fallplot2 <- ggplot(fallmelt, aes(WEEK, value/1000, linetype = variable,
                    colour = variable)) + geom_line(size = 1) +
                    theme_bw()  +

                    opts(title="Fall Cumulative") +

                    labs(y="Number of fish (1000s)", x = 'WEEK')

# Modified call - I just reset ymin and ymax so that the color would map
# throughout the y-scale. The values in scale_fill_manual() are what got
# it to work for me, but it messed up the variable legend in the process :(

fallplot2 + geom_rect(aes(NULL, NULL, xmin = start, xmax = end,
    fill = year), data = ydata, ymin = 0, ymax = 20000) +
      scale_fill_manual(values = alpha(c('blue', 'gray50'), 0.01),
                      legend = FALSE)  +
      scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(1,52,3),labels=levels(fall$week)
                [seq(1,52,3)],)

Hope this is of some assistance.
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for those links, but I ended up going in a different direction
using the gpclib library.

cities <- structure(list(CitState = c("SiouxFalls SD", "Rockford IL",
"Kenosha WI",
"Duluth MN", "SiouxCity IA", "CedarRapids IA", "NewYork NY"),
    Latitude = c(43.54599, 42.265973, 42.577791, 46.779135,
42.489678,
    41.976662, 40.756054), Longitude = c(-96.731291, -89.086667,
    -87.822644, -92.108243, -96.404948, -91.673155, -73.986951
    )), .Names = c("CitState", "Latitude", "Longitude"), row.names =
c(1L,
2L, 3L, 4L, 5L, 6L, 267L), class = "data.frame")

library(maps)

library(deldir)
library(gpclib)

us <- data.frame(map("usa", regions = "main",plot = F)[c("x","y")])
manhattan <- data.frame(map("usa", regions = "manhattan",plot = F)
[c("x","y")])

longisland <- data.frame(map("usa", regions = "long island",plot = F)

[c("x","y")])

cities.tess <- deldir(cities$Longitude, cities$Latitude)

clip.border <- function(deldir.obj, border){
	require(gpclib)
	bord <- as(matrix(ncol = 2), "gpc.poly")
	for(i in seq(along = border)){
		b <- as(border[[i]], "gpc.poly")
		bord <- union(b, bord)
	}

	tiles <- tile.list(deldir.obj)
	out <- {}
	group <- 1
	for(i in seq(along = tiles)){
		poly <- cbind(tiles[[i]]$x, tiles[[i]]$y)
		poly <- as(poly, "gpc.poly")

		poly <- intersect(poly, bord)
		if(length(poly@pts)>0){
			for(j in seq(along=poly@pts)){
				poly.df <- data.frame(x = poly@pts[[j]]$x, y =poly@pts[[j]]$y)
				poly.df$ID <- i
				poly.df$group <- group
				group <- group + 1
				out <- rbind(out, poly.df)
			}
		}
	}
	return(out)
}

tess.df <- clip.border(cities.tess, list(us, manhattan, longisland))
tess.df$CitState <- cities[tess.df$ID,]$CitState

ggplot(tess.df, aes(x,y)) + geom_polygon(aes(group = group,fill =
CitState))+coord_map()

messages.body_plain:
Here's a few more tweaks to get your the whole way:

ggplot(fallmelt, aes(WEEK, value/1000, linetype = variable,
    colour = variable)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +

  geom_rect(data = ydata, inherit.aes = FALSE, legend = FALSE,
    aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, fill = year, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = alpha(c('blue', 'gray50'), 0.1), legend = F)

Note the use of Inf and legend = FALSE in the layer.

Hadley

messages.subject: Putting titles on facets
messages.body_plain:
Hello Folks,

Last week I asked a question to Hadley and he suggested I asked it here.

Since then, I’ve solved the problem, but he solution is quite fiddly.

Any suggestion is appreciated.

Here is the problem:

 Looking at facet_grid:

p <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(carat, ..density..)) +   geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2)

p + facet_grid(clarity ~ cut)

If I want to put a title on “clarity”, I can do:

p + facet_grid(clarity ~ cut) +opts(title="Clarity")

But is there a simpler way of Putting a Title on the Facets?

I’d like to put “Cut” as the title of the cut facet…

So what I thought was:

# Setting the Theme

theme_set(theme_bw())

# Creating Viewports

VP<- viewport(width=1,height=1, x=0.5,y=0.5)

VP2<- viewport(width=.8,height=.8, x=0.5,y=0.5)

# Creating a Blank plot, witht he title and Facet Y label

OutPlot<- ggplot(diamonds, aes(carat, price))+geom_blank()+opts(title="Plot title",

panel.grid.major=theme_blank(), panel.grid.minor=theme_blank(), panel.border =theme_blank(),

axis.text.x=theme_text(colour= "white"),axis.text.y=theme_text(colour= "white"),

axis.title.x=theme_text(colour= "white"), axis.title.y=theme_text(colour= "white"),

axis.line=theme_segment(colour= "white"),axis.ticks=theme_segment(colour= "white"))+geom_text(aes(x=5, y=10000),angle=90,label="Facet Y label")

# Defining the inner plot as in The help example

p <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(carat, ..density..)) +   geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2)

# Defining the Ineer plot

InPlot <- p + facet_grid(clarity ~ cut)+opts(title="Facet X label", strip.background = theme_blank())

windows()

print(OutPlot, vp=VP)

print(InPlot, vp=VP2)

I just want to make this simpler….

Thanks

Marcelo

messages.subject: Re: changing line charactistics for density plot
messages.subject_clean: changing line charactistics for density plot
messages.body_plain:
Just as color is controlled with the colour aesthetic, line type and
thickness are controlled by the size and linetype aesthetics.  See
http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/geom_density.html  These can either be set to
a single value outside the aes call, or mapped to a variable inside
it.

If  you need more help than this, a reproducible example would be
necessary to show what you have done and are trying to do

--Brian Diggs

ggplot from stat="density".

Rob

messages.subject: RE: Putting titles on facets
messages.body_plain:
Dear baptiste,
Thanks for that....

Yesterday I had a few ideas and came up with a nice solution.
Hope it is useful for everyone...

p <- ggplot(diamonds, aes(carat, ..density..)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.2)

VP <- viewport(width=0.95,height=0.95, x=0.0,y=0.0, just=c(0,0))
InPlot <- p + facet_grid(clarity ~ cut)+opts(title="X facet label", strip.background = theme_blank())
print(InPlot, vp=VP)
grid.text("Y facet Label" ,x=0.95,y=0.5,rot = 270)
grid.text("Graph Title", x=0.5, y=0.95, gp=gpar(fontsize=14))

Cheers
Marcelo

-----Original Message-----
From: baptiste auguie [mailto:bapt...@googlemail.com]
Sent: Monday, 17 May 2010 22:09
To: Marcelo Stabile
Cc: ggp...@googlegroups.com
Subject: Re: Putting titles on facets

Hi,

Try this,

p = qplot(hp, wt, data=mtcars,facets=vs ~ am ) + opts(title = "Facet X label")
source("http://gridextra.googlecode.com/svn/trunk/R/arrange.r")
arrange(p, main = textGrob("Plot title", gp=gpar(fontface
="bold",fontsize=12)),
               legend = textGrob("Facet Y label",rot=90,gp=gpar(fontsize=14)))

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Bullet graph in ggplot2?
messages.body_plain:
Try this one for your bar solution:

fake.data <- data.frame(measure=letters[1:10], value=rpois(10,5),
mean=rpois(10,5), target=rpois(10,5) )
p <- ggplot(fake.data, aes(measure, value) )
p <- p + geom_bar(fill="grey", width=0.5)
p <- p + geom_bar(aes(measure, mean), width=0.2)
p <- p + geom_point(aes(measure, target), colour="red")

p <- p + geom_errorbar(aes(y = target,x = measure, ymin = target,ymax
= target), width = .45)

p <- p + coord_flip()
p

cheers
Gerry

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am new to ggplot, and really like the package. However, I
encountered an error when trying to put two plots in the same pdf.
Here is my plotting funtion:

plotActMod <- function (dat, letter, path = '.')
{
  for (let in letter) {
    modnam <- paste('mod', let, 'pct', sep = '_')
    actnam <- paste('act', let, 'pct', sep = '_')
    capx <- paste(toupper(let), 'modified percentile score', sep = '
')
    capy <- paste(toupper(let), 'actual percentile score', sep = ' ')
		# do the pdf
		pdf(paste(path, '/', let, '-scatterNcontour.pdf', sep = ''),
				width = 12, height = 6)
		par(mfrow = 1:2)
    p <- ggplot(dat, aes(modnam, actnam, check.names = FALSE))
    print(p + geom_point(position = position_jitter(height = 1, width
= 1),
                    colour = alpha('darkorchid3', 0.85))
     			+ labs(x = capx, y = capy))
		# now do a contour plot
    cont <- .prepContourDat(dat, 'mod_d_pct', 'act_d_pct', 17, 17)
    v <- ggplot(cont, aes(x = mod_d_pct, y = act_d_pct, z = count))
    print(v + stat_contour(colour = alpha('darkorchid3', 0.85), size =
1.1)
          + labs(x = capx, y = capy))
		graphics.off()
  }
	# finito
}

And here is the error I get:
> plotActMod(dat = dat, letter = 'd', path = '../../graphics')
Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'modnam' not found

Note that if I do not use print() within the function, I do not get
this error, but the output is not a valid .pdf file. Seems like this
is a scoping issue. Please help work around it. Thank you!

Sergiy

> dfrmsdmelt <- melt(dfrmsd)
> theme_set(theme_bw())   # white background

the "alpha=(0.2)" out of the aes() call and just make it another

implies that you want to create a scale for alpha, and a scale (by

I don't know why this would be dependent on theme, though.

messages.subject: Re: help for labels_bquote
messages.body_plain:
Got it, thanks for your help Baptiste -- label_bquote is actually what I
need, because my facet labels are something like: X, Y, Z, and I wanted
to have something like X_a, Y_a, Z_a on the figure, so the following
will do this in one step:

... + facet_grid( ~ fac, labeller = label_bquote(.(x)_a ) )

This avoids me having to rename all the labels manually, so it is an
example where label_bquote is clearly useful.

Etienne

messages.subject_clean: problem with making multiple plots (geom_pointrange) in a loop
messages.body_plain:
G'day,

This is just a guess, but I think you might be running into a memory
or internal memory allocation ceiling within R.  I encountered a
similar error when trying to save a hi-res (1200 dpi) bitmap through
ggsave under Windows XP.  Sometimes it would generate the same error
as you are getting, sometimes not.  After some experimenting, I
reduced the resolution back to 300 dpi  ( which is still generating a
4mb file) and problem solved.  Even though you are saving jpeg's,
presumably it is being generated by shrinking a bitmap. Try varying
dimensions and dpi in ggsave and see if that helps.
cheers
Gerry

Gerry

messages.subject: stat_bin2d with geom_text
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a question that is related to Rob's: (see below)

How can I use geoms other than "rect" with stat_bin2d?

I have tried

stat_bin2d(geom="text", aes(x=x, y=y, label=..count..), bins=3)

but it doesn't work.

Reproducible code:

df <- data.frame(v1=runif(2000), v2=runif(2000))
pl <- ggplot(df) + xlim(c(0,1)) + ylim(c(0,1))

# This works of course:
pl + stat_bin2d(geom="rect", aes(x=v1, y=v2, fill=..count..), bins=3)

# But:
pl + stat_bin2d(geom="text", aes(x=v1, y=v2, label=..count..), bins=3)

# gives the Error: geom_text requires the following missing aesthetics: x, y

pl + stat_bin2d(geom="point", aes(x=v1, y=v2, size=..count..), bins=3)

pl + stat_bin2d(geom="text", aes(x=..xmax.., y=..ymax.., label=..count..), bins=3)

What am I getting wrong here?

The idea behind this is to create a colour coded kind of "confusion matrix" reprsenting the correlation between two biological assays with continuous readouts between 0 and 1.

I am looking for a possibility to create autocorrelation plots comparable to those plotted by acf().

I have plotted my ts nicely with qplot, like this:

thx in advance for any help, best

matt

In that case, you'll need to do something like:

all.data <- transform(all.data,
  binx = round_any(x, 10),
  biny = round_any(y, 10)
)
sum.data <- ddply(all.data, c("binx", "biny"), summarise,
  n = length(binx),  qual = mean(qual), .progress = "text")

And then plot the results of sum.data with bin2d.

messages.subject_clean: showing only centroid value (or mean of X and Y)?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I would like to know if there is a way in ggplot2 to plot the central
value of a group of points (or the mean on X and Y). With the data I
use, it get's to dense in some regions and since I have one factor
with 8 levels, it get's confusing with different colors (and worse
with different shapes).

I see that stat_summary seems to point out to what I would like to do,
but how to do it on both X and Y. I do not want to plot the original
data, but only the central value.

Here's a small example with qplot. I've used one factor with 2 levels,
and the other with 5.

val_x = runif(40,0,1)
val_y = rnorm(40,0,1)
fact1 = rep(1:2,each=20)
fact2 = rep(1:5,8)

test = qplot(val_x,val_y, shape=factor(fact1),colour=factor(fact2))

Thank you all for your help.

guillaume

Ph.D. candidate --- Plant Biology
Université Laval, Québec, QC, Canada
guillaume.ther...@ulaval.ca

messages.subject: Re: acf, autocorrelation plot with ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
FYI there is a fortify method for "tis" time series in the "tis" package.  See ?fortify.tis

The package also has some functions to convert between some of the other time series classes,
 i.e. you can use fortify(as.tis(some.ts.series)) to fortify the basic "ts" series used in base R.

- Trevor

Hi Raj,

It's the same as the other plotting systems in R: you need to change
the order of the underlying factor levels.  e.g.:

levels(diamonds$color) <- c("J", "D", "E", "I", "H", "F", "G")

Hadley

messages.subject: acf plotting function for ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have written a function to plot autocorrelation with ggplot2 similar
to the way the standard acf function does. Probably there´s some
niftier way to do it, but maybe it can help someone else, too.
Certainly the result looks better than the standard acf plot.  If you
have any suggestions, hints, general advice - I am happy to learn it.

Here´s the function:

#### two supporting functions...
###  the first support function is just to crop the result of acf in
order to get a result that can be processed easily by lapply and
as.data.frame

ret_acf =function(x){
	a=acf(x,plot=FALSE,lag.max=length(x))
	return(a$acf)
	}

### this calculates the CI threshold the same like acf does.
calc_ci = function(ci,n){

		a=c(qnorm((1 + 0.95)/2)/sqrt(n),qnorm((1 + 0.95)/2)/sqrt(n)*(-1))

		return(a)

		}

## this is a simple function that accepts dataframes containing one or
more timeseries and returns a facet grid plot of all the series in the
frame. plotting paramaters (alpha, color etc.) could also be added to
these arguments

ggplot_acf =function(dframe,ci){

	r=lapply(dframe,"ret_acf")
	r=as.data.frame(r)
	r=cbind(1:dim(r)[1],r)
	names(r)[1]="lag"

	r=melt(r,id="lag")

q=qplot(lag,value,data=r,geom="bar",stat="identity",position="identity",ylab="acf",main="Autocorrelations")
+ facet_grid(variable~.) +geom_hline(yintercept=calc_ci(ci=ci,n=dim(r)
[1]),color="blue",size=0.1)
+geom_hline(yintercept=calc_ci(ci=ci,n=dim(r)
[1])*(-1),color="blue",size=0.1)
+geom_hline(yintercept=0,color="red",alpha=0.9,size=0.2)

	return(q)

		}

best

matt

--

messages.body_plain:
Hi Guillaume,

There's no way to do this purely in ggplot2, but it's pretty easy to
summarise the data yourself:

library(ggplot2)
df <- data.frame(
  val_x = runif(40,0,1),
  val_y = rnorm(40,0,1),
  fact1 = factor(rep(1:2,each=20)),
  fact2 = factor(rep(1:5,8)))

qplot(val_x,val_y, shape = fact1, colour = fact2, data = df)

mid <- ddply(df, c("fact1", "fact2"), summarise,
  val_x = mean(val_x), val_y = mean(val_y))

qplot(val_x,val_y, shape = fact1, colour = fact2, data = df) +
  geom_point(data = mid, size = 5)

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: stat_bin2d with geom_text
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, May 19, 2010 at 8:48 AM, <sebastia...@basf.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I have a question that is related to Rob's: (see below)
>
> How can I use geoms other than "rect" with stat_bin2d?
>
> I have tried
>
> stat_bin2d(geom="text", aes(x=x, y=y, label=..count..), bins=3)
>
> but it doesn't work.
>
> Reproducible code:
>
> df <- data.frame(v1=runif(2000), v2=runif(2000))
> pl <- ggplot(df) + xlim(c(0,1)) + ylim(c(0,1))
>
> # This works of course:
> pl + stat_bin2d(geom="rect", aes(x=v1, y=v2, fill=..count..), bins=3)
>
>
> # But:
> pl + stat_bin2d(geom="text", aes(x=v1, y=v2, label=..count..), bins=3)
>
> # gives the Error: geom_text requires the following missing aesthetics: x, y

You get this error because stat_bin2d is optimised to work with
geom_rect - it returns xmin, xmax, ymin and ymax aesthetics, not the x
and y aesthetics that geom_text needs.  There's no simple alternative
except to do the summarisation yourself.

Hadley

messages.subject: Problem adding expressions to plots
messages.body_plain:
Given the appended example i have two questions:
1. How can i preserve the space after "log " in the expression for
ystr? It does not show up in the axis label.
2. I would like to add some results to the graph. I used substitute to
replace val in the expression. However, doing so, i get an error
message in the geom_text statement (missing label).

Thanks,
Herbert
----------------------------
xmin=0
xmax=100
df <- data.frame(x=c(xmin:xmax), y=c(xmax:xmin))

xstr <- expression('Time (s)')
ystr <- expression('Intensity (log ' * cd/m^2 * ')')
p <- ggplot(df) +
    scale_x_continuous(name=xstr, limits=c(xmin, xmax), expand=c(0,
0)) +
    scale_y_continuous(name=ystr, limits=c(xmin, xmax), expand=c(0,
0)) +
    geom_point(aes(x, y))

tres <- 5 # result from calculation
tt <- substitute(
                 expression('Threshold: ' * val * 'log ' * cd/m^2),
                 list(val=tres))
p <- p + geom_text(aes(x=(xmin+xmax)/2, y=2, label=tt))
print(p)

messages.subject: Change order facet_wrap
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Here is my question.

I am drawing a graph with 8 panels with qplot and use the function facet_wrap to maximize the graph space:
facet_wrap(~ Site, ncol = 3)
The graph structure by default is the following (p.116 ggplot2 book):
1   2   3
4   5   6
7   8   9
But if there is only 8 panels to draw, then the last panel is empty (only 8 sites not 9) but still
the labels (ticks and numbers) are shown for this empty panel (as the example in p.121 ggplot2 book).
Is it possible to change the order by which the grids are filled (so that the empty panel will be the upper right one, without ticks and numbers)?  For example.

7   8   9
4   5   6
1   2   3

Or is it possible to remove the ticks and numbers of a selected panel?

Thank you in advance.

Yann

messages.subject: Re: Problem adding expressions to plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi Herbert,

You want something like this:

tt <- paste('"Threshold: " * ', tres,  " * ' log ' * cd/m^2", sep = "")
p + annotate("text", x = (xmin+xmax)/2, y = 2, label=tt, parse = TRUE)

Currently there's no easy way to include expressions in data frames
(which is the internal structure that ggplot2 uses to handle all data)
so you need to pass in a string and then tell geom_text to parse it
into an expression.  Also note the use of annotate so you don't get
the same label drawn repeatedly for every observation in the original
dataset.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: xlim(), stat_bin, the group aesthetic and discrete scales
messages.subject_clean: xlim(), stat_bin, the group aesthetic and discrete scales
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, May 11, 2010 at 12:51 PM, John Rauser <jra...@gmail.com> wrote:
> (Trying a more specific list, apologies to r-help@ subscribers that may have
> already seen this.)
>
> I'm a new ggplot user and am really loving it so far, but I have run into a
> little trouble.  I'm hoping someone here can clarify.
>
> I've been plotting histograms of discrete variables like so:
>
>> df<-data.frame(names=c("Bob","Mary","Joe","Bob","Bob"))
>> p<-ggplot(df,aes(names))
>> p+geom_histogram()
>
> But sometimes I want to constrain the categories (the factor in my real
> dataset has many, many levels).  When I do this in (what seems like) the
> simplest way I get an error:
>
>> p+geom_histogram()+xlim("Bob","Mary")
> Error in data.frame(count = as.numeric(tapply(weight, bins, sum, na.rm =
> TRUE))$
>   arguments imply differing number of rows: 0, 1
>
> If I use xlim() to specify all the levels, or all the levels plus a few
> extra levels, things work as expected:
>
>> p+geom_histogram()+xlim("Bob","Mary","Joe")
>> p+geom_histogram()+xlim("Bob","Mary","Joe","Frank")
>
> I found the error surprising because I had been successfully plotting
> ..density.. instead of the default ..count.. and constraining the x-axis
> like so:
>
>> p+geom_histogram(aes(y=..density..,group=1))+xlim("Bob","Mary")
>
> After some experimentation, I've come to the conclusion that using the group
> aesthetic is the key to successfully using xlim() with stat_bin and discrete
> scales.  That is, the following does what I want:
>
> p+geom_histogram(aes(group=1))+xlim("Bob","Mary")
>
> I have two questions:
>
> 1) Is this expected behavior?  The interaction of the group aesthetic and
> discrete scale manipulation seems unintuitive to me, but perhaps this is
> because I'm a ggplot novice.

Definitely not - this is a small bug in stat_bin which will be fixed
in the next version.  I will probably rewrite stat_bin in some point
in the future to be much more efficient - currently it's a bit slow,
particularly if you have a large number of discrete values and haven't
set group = 1.

> 2) More generally, how do people debug gpplot commands?  When I get a
> cryptic error message like the above it's nearly always because I've asked
> for something unreasonable, but if often takes me a long time and lots of
> experimentation to spot my error. Do folks have any ggplot debugging tips?

Unfortunately not :(  I look at the output of tr() and then add in
browser() statements where I think the problem is likely to be, but
that's probably not helpful for most people.

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
Hello

Because I want to produce EPS and PDF files with embedded true type
fonts that I've installed on my system, I'm using the Cairo graphics
device. Unfortunately, rotated axis labels are out of alignment when
I'm using non-standard fonts.

Try this:
library(ggplot2)
library(Cairo)
df <- data.frame(y=1:2, x=c('a', 'bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb'))
CairoPDF()
ggplot(df,aes(x=x, y=y))+geom_bar()+
opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(angle=45,hjust=1,family='Times'))
dev.off()
shell.exec(paste(getwd(), 'Rplots.pdf', sep = '/'))

Is this a bug of ggplot2 or of the Cairo graphics device?

Erich

messages.body_plain:
You are so close! Your points are filled but the errorbars get plotted
on top, just change the order:

p = ggplot(df, aes(val_x, val_y, fill=factor(fact1), shape=factor(fact2))) +

scale_shape_manual(values=c(22,23,24,25,21)) +
scale_fill_manual(values=c("1"="white", "2"="black")) + theme_bw() +
geom_errorbar(p.ylim, size=0.5) +

geom_errorbarh(p.xlim, size=0.5) +
geom_point(size = 4)

You use height to change the end bars on geom_errorbarh but due to a
bug it needs to be inside aes.  So, you'll need to change:

p.xlim = aes(xmin = val_x - er_x, xmax = val_x + er_x, height = 0.5)

Charlotte

messages.body_plain:

ggplot2. I thought I'd aggregate the possibilities here and publicise
them, just in case you're in a giving mode ;)

    Cost: zero. Effort: low

    when you publish your work. You can get the citation by running

    It helps to let my department know directly that you're finding
    my work useful. The easiest way to do that would be to send a letter
    to my chair, Kathy Ensor, at the address below.

    Kathy Ensor
    Professor and Chair of Statistics
    Department of Statistics, MS 138
    Rice University
    P.O. Box 1892
    Houston, TX 77251-1892

    Cost: low. Effort: low.

    I love getting packages ;)
    http://amazon.com/gp/registry/1Y65N3VFA613B

    Cost: medium.  Effort: medium.

messages.subject: Re: plotting multiple data frame columns??
messages.body_plain:
I also tend to use ggplot() rather than qplot(), for the same reason
as Ben.  However, there are two ways to achieve your objective using
qplot().

The first to add a new layer for each additional column in your
data.frame.

df <- data.frame(x=c(1:10), y1=c(10:1), y2=c(1:10))

qplot(df$x, df$y1, geom="line") + geom_line(aes(y=df$y2))

The second way is to reshape your data into a long dataframe, as
opposed to a wide dataframe, and then using the group= parameter in
qplot:

library(reshape)

df <- data.frame(x=c(1:10), y1=c(10:1), y2=c(1:10))

mdf <- melt(df, id.vars="x")
qplot(x, value, group=variable, data=mdf, geom="line")

Andrie

Thanks kindly to Dennis, Andrie & Ben!  I keep forgetting about
melt(), which I know is quite handy.  And as folks said above, simply
using the geom_line() twice works great.  Thanks!

    Now if I may follow up with another question:  I usually stay away
from ggplot (as opposed to qplot) because it seems less forgiving in
that it forces you to use a data frame more often.  As I show above, I
like to call the "x" column df$x and provide it as a vector instead of
as just the data frame column name.  There are 2 reasons why I
currently prefer qplot:

(1) It allows for more flexibility:  I don't have to have all of my
columns of interest in the same data frame (or in a data frame at all)

need to provide the data frame & then put the NAME of the column in
the aes.  Is there any way around this?  If so, I will always use
ggplot, like the others above.  E.g., is there any way to write:

ggplot(df, aes(x=time, y=eval(i))

or even better:

ggplot(aes(x=df$time, y=df[,i]))      (ignoring the required dataframe
somehow)

I know that "eval" is not the right function for my call above.  But
is there something that exists to fix this?  I really like the ggplot2
package, it is amazing.  But this reliance upon data frames &
especially upon column names is a serious Achilles' heel.

messages.subject: Re: plotting multiple data frame columns??
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Using ggplot in a loop is quite easy with aes_string, or subsetting,
or a melted data.frame. Consider this example where we want to plot n
data.frames, n=1, 2, 3, and for each one we want to plot the n+1-th
column against x. Below are three solutions:

l <- replicate(3, data.frame(x = 1:10,
                             y1 = rnorm(10),
                             y2 = rnorm(10),
                             y3 = rnorm(10)), simplify=FALSE)

library(ggplot2)

p <- list()
for( ii in seq_along(l)){

  yname <- names(l[[ii]])[ii+1]
  p[[ii]] <- ggplot(l[[ii]]) +
    geom_path(aes_string(x="x", y=yname))

}

p2 <- list()
for( ii in seq_along(l)){

  tmp <- subset(l[[ii]], select=c(1, ii+1))
  names(tmp) <- c("x", "y")
  p2[[ii]] <- ggplot(tmp) +
    geom_path(aes(x, y))

}

## test
## do.call(arrange, p2)

m <- melt(l, id="x")
p3 <- dlply(subset(m, as.numeric(variable) == L1), .(L1), function(d){
  print(  str(d))
  ggplot(d) +
    geom_path(aes(x, value))
})

## test
## do.call(arrange, p3)

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject_clean: showing only centroid value (or mean of X and Y)?
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

You can probably use stat_something to do this more elegantly and
fiddle with the scales, but if you summarize the data before calling
ggplot(), you can sometimes save yourself some work.

I chose to get the average horsepower before going to ggplot(), setting the
result up as a factor with values rounded to two decimal places and named so
that I wouldn't have to resort to using scale_fill_* later on to change the legend title:

mtcars2 <- ddply(mtcars, .(cyl), transform, AvgHP = factor(round(mean(hp), 2)))
p <- ggplot(mtcars2, aes(factor(cyl), mpg))
p + geom_boxplot(aes(fill = AvgHP))

If you prefer the scale to be on a gradient instead, remove the factor() specification
in the definition of AvgHP in mtcars2, in which case the rounding isn't really
necessary. I prefer the version above because it displays the mean horsepower
per cylinder size in the graph, but your purposes may be different.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Scaling & Stats Bug
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, May 7, 2010 at 5:17 PM, Sala <salathe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hey all
>
> I continue to run into problems with logs. Let's say I have a simple
> data frame, like
>
> df = data.frame(x=c(1,1,1),y=c(1,0,0.5))
>
> The mean of df$y is 0.5:
>
>> mean(df$y)
> [1] 0.5
>
> Plotting this with a log10 transformed y axis shows an incorrect value
> (somewhere around 10^-0.33):
>
>> ggplot(df,aes(x,y)) + stat_summary(fun.y=mean, geom="point") + scale_y_continuous(trans="log10")

It's a bit hard to see what's going wrong here.  Adding some more
information and tweaking values makes things a bit easier:

df <- data.frame(x = 1,y = c(50,100,150))

ggplot(df,aes(x,y)) +
  geom_point() +
  stat_summary(fun.y=mean, geom="point", color = "red") +
  scale_y_log10()

Why doesn't the red dot lie at 10^2?  Well, the scale transformation
occurs before the statistical transformation - so we're computing the
mean of the log transformed values:

> mean(log10(c(50, 100, 150)))
[1] 1.958354

It works this way because the basic idea is that these two plots
should appear identical (apart from the labels on the scale):

ggplot(df,aes(x,y)) +
  geom_point() +
  stat_summary(fun.y=mean, geom="point", color = "red") +
  scale_y_log10()

and

ggplot(df,aes(x, log10(y))) +
  geom_point() +
  stat_summary(fun.y=mean, geom="point", color = "red")

Does that help?

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: Put two plots side by side
messages.subject_clean: Put two plots side by side
messages.body_plain:
Two different ways:
library(ggplot2)
x=5
size=50
A=data.frame(X=sample(x, size, replace=T), Y=sample(x, size, replace=T),a=rep(1:2,each=25));A
# Facetting
qplot(X,Y,data=A) + geom_jitter(position=position_jitter(width=.03)) + facet_grid(.~a)
# Or with vp

p=qplot(X, Y, data=A) + geom_jitter(position=position_jitter(width=.03))
ggsave(p, file='main.png')
p1=qplot(X, Y, data=A) + geom_jitter(position=position_jitter(width=.3))

ggsave(p1, file='main2.png')
vport <- function(x, y)
viewport(layout.pos.row=x, layout.pos.col=y)
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(1,2)))
print(p, vp=vport(1,1))
print(p1, vp=vport(1,2))
